tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Five lines from a central bank's policy commentary. Decide whether each phrase is the combination monetary-policy writing actually uses.
statements: Policymakers voted to harden monetary policy after core inflation proved unexpectedly sticky.
The committee's guidance was designed to anchor inflation expectations before the autumn wage round.
Officials insisted that a further quarter-point rise would not provoke a soft landing in the labour market.
The bank continued to withdraw liquidity out of the money market through weekly repo operations.
Rate-setters said they would hold the ground on rates until inflation returned to target.
tasks.solution_overview: Central-bank prose is unusually formulaic, so each line can be checked against the phrase a published policy statement would print. Watch which verbs belong with the stance itself, which belong with expectations, and which belong with operations in the money market, because each of those three slots has its own settled partner. Two of the traps here are blends of two genuine idioms, so say the whole phrase aloud and ask which half has been borrowed from somewhere else.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Policymakers voted to harden monetary policy after core inflation proved unexpectedly sticky.**

Monetary policy is tightened or loosened, and that antonym pair is fixed: a tightening cycle, an easing cycle, tighter conditions. "Harden" governs attitudes and positions rather than instruments — a stance hardens, a line hardens, rhetoric hardens — so it cannot take the policy setting itself as its object. Sticky core inflation is exactly the trigger a tightening decision reports, which shows the noun and the reason are right and only the verb has slipped.

**Trap:** A hawkish tone can harden; the policy it announces tightens.

The decision described is a rate rise in response to persistent inflation, so the wording a minute would carry is "voted to tighten monetary policy."

**B) The committee's guidance was designed to anchor inflation expectations before the autumn wage round.**

Expectations are anchored, and the metaphor is so entrenched that its failure has its own name: de-anchored expectations. Guidance is the standard instrument credited with doing the anchoring, since the point of publishing a path for rates is to fix what households and firms assume about future prices. Wage bargaining is in turn the classic channel through which those assumptions become actual inflation.

Verb, object and timing all sit inside one settled frame here, so the sentence reads exactly as a policy commentary would write it.

**C) Officials insisted that a further quarter-point rise would not provoke a soft landing in the labour market.**

A soft landing is engineered, achieved or delivered, because the phrase names the outcome policymakers are steering towards: inflation falls without a collapse in employment. "Provoke" governs unwelcome reactions — provoke a backlash, provoke a sell-off, provoke a run — so attaching it to the one result every central banker wants inverts the evaluation the sentence needs.

**Trap:** The verb, not the noun, carries the judgement; check whether the outcome is desired before choosing it.

Officials were reassuring their audience rather than disowning a success, so the line they would actually give is "would still deliver a soft landing in the labour market."

**D) The bank continued to withdraw liquidity out of the money market through weekly repo operations.**

Liquidity is drained from a market or withdrawn from it, and the mirror image is injecting liquidity into it; the operational vocabulary keeps to that in-and-out pair with "from" and "into." "Out of" belongs to physical extraction — tipping water out of a jug — and after "withdraw" the settled preposition is simply "from."

**Tip:** Inject liquidity into a market, drain it from one.

The repo operations described are the standard way of absorbing cash, so the phrase an operations desk would use is "drain liquidity from the money market."

**E) Rate-setters said they would hold the ground on rates until inflation returned to target.**

Two real idioms have been welded together here: "hold the line on rates," which is what a committee does when it refuses to move, and "stand one's ground," which is what a person does under pressure. Each is fine on its own, but "hold the ground" belongs to neither, and the military sense of holding ground needs territory rather than a policy setting.

The committee is refusing to shift its rate until a condition is met, so the natural version is "hold the line on rates until inflation returned to target."

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Five lines from a labour-market briefing on shortages and pay. Decide whether each verb sits with its noun the way employment economics words it.
statements: A shrinking pool of applicants has narrowed the labour market in several regions.
Two years of rapid inflation ate away real wages across the private sector.
Vacancy data suggest that acute skill shortages are bidding up wages in construction.
The minimum wage increase was expected to squeeze out the wage premium enjoyed by shift supervisors.
Firms facing chronic shortages have begun to poach staff from smaller regional rivals.
tasks.solution_overview: Labour economics describes scarcity, pay erosion and competition for staff with a small set of verbs that have hardened into terms of art. Ask what English does to a market when workers are scarce, what inflation does to the buying power of pay, and what happens to the differential between two grades when the floor rises. One trap is a missing preposition rather than a wrong verb, so read each phrase for its complete pattern and not just its headline word.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A shrinking pool of applicants has narrowed the labour market in several regions.**

A labour market tightens when workers are scarce and loosens when they are plentiful, and the adjective follows the same logic in "a tight labour market." "Narrow" needs an object with two measurable edges — a gap, a lead, a spread, a margin — and a market is not that sort of object, which is why nobody reports a narrow labour market either.

**Tip:** Gaps narrow; markets tighten.

The sentence describes scarcity pushing employers into competition, so the standard reading is "has tightened the labour market in several regions."

**B) Two years of rapid inflation ate away real wages across the private sector.**

Inflation erodes real wages, or eats away at them, and that second phrase is fixed with its preposition: "eat away" never governs a bare object. Removing "at" leaves a pattern English does not have, even though the metaphor of slow consumption is the right one for what rising prices do to the purchasing power of pay.

**Trap:** Eat into and eat away at both need their preposition; only the plain verb eat takes a direct object.

The sense is right but the pattern is broken, so the sentence needs "ate away at real wages" or, in more formal reporting, "eroded real wages."

**C) Vacancy data suggest that acute skill shortages are bidding up wages in construction.**

When competing buyers force a price higher, English says they bid it up, and the phrase transfers from auctions to housing, commodities and labour without changing shape. Shortages are the standard subject of that verb in pay reporting, because scarce skills are precisely what rival employers compete over, and vacancy figures are the evidence normally cited for the claim.

The mechanism and the phrase that names it match exactly here, so the wording is what a labour-market briefing would print.

**D) The minimum wage increase was expected to squeeze out the wage premium enjoyed by shift supervisors.**

A differential is compressed or eroded when a rising floor catches up with the grade above it, and "wage compression" is the technical name for that effect. "Squeeze out" means to force something or someone out of a market altogether — smaller rivals get squeezed out — so it describes expulsion rather than the shrinking of a gap.

What the rise threatens is the size of the supervisors' advantage rather than its existence, so the line should read "compress the wage premium enjoyed by shift supervisors."

**E) Firms facing chronic shortages have begun to poach staff from smaller regional rivals.**

Poaching is the settled term for hiring away another employer's workers, and it keeps the preposition "from" for the firm that loses them. The word carries a mild accusation of unfairness, which fits a sentence about large employers turning on smaller competitors during a shortage.

Both the verb and the pattern around it are the ones this situation calls for, so the sentence stands as competent reporting.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Five lines from coverage of a company's results season. Decide whether each phrase matches the wording of financial reporting.
statements: The retailer made a profit warning three weeks before the Christmas trading update.
Management admitted that the write-down would dent operating margins in the second half.
Quarterly revenue overtook analysts' forecasts by the widest margin in three years.
The board declined to reinstate the dividend until leverage fell below two times earnings.
Auditors questioned whether the group had been smoothing earnings across reporting periods.
tasks.solution_overview: Results reporting runs on announcements, comparisons and payout decisions, each with its own fixed verb. Ask which announcements are issued rather than made, what a company does when figures come in above the consensus, and what happens to a dividend that was suspended and is now restored. Two of the phrases are technical accounting terms, so judge them on what the practice actually is rather than on how the words sound.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The retailer made a profit warning three weeks before the Christmas trading update.**

A profit warning is issued, and that verb covers the whole family of formal market announcements: firms issue guidance, issue a statement, issue a trading update. "Make" governs the outcome itself rather than the announcement of it, which is why a company makes a profit but issues the warning that it will not.

**Tip:** Make the result, issue the announcement about it.

What the retailer released was a formal notice to the market, so the phrase financial pages use is "issued a profit warning."

**B) Management admitted that the write-down would dent operating margins in the second half.**

Margins are dented, squeezed, eroded or wiped out, and "dent" is the mild member of that set: it signals visible but survivable damage rather than collapse. A write-down is exactly the sort of one-off charge that produces that scale of effect, and pairing it with the softest verb in the family is how management would play the news down.

The strength of the verb matches the size of the event it reports, so the sentence works as written.

**C) Quarterly revenue overtook analysts' forecasts by the widest margin in three years.**

Results beat, exceed or come in ahead of forecasts, and "beat expectations" is so standard that a results-day headline barely needs anything else. "Overtake" requires two things travelling in the same direction, one catching the other, which is why cars and runners overtake but figures compared at a single moment do not.

**Trap:** A forecast is a benchmark, not a moving rival, so the verb of pursuit does not fit.

The comparison is between one quarter's figure and the consensus estimate for it, so the line should read "beat analysts' forecasts by the widest margin in three years."

**D) The board declined to reinstate the dividend until leverage fell below two times earnings.**

A dividend is cut, suspended or passed when a company is under strain, and reinstated when it resumes; "reinstate" carries exactly the sense of restoring something that was previously withdrawn. Tying that restoration to a leverage test is the usual condition boards attach, since lenders expect debt to come down before cash flows back to shareholders.

The verb presupposes a payment that had been stopped, which is precisely the situation described, so this line reads as a competent results report.

**E) Auditors questioned whether the group had been smoothing earnings across reporting periods.**

Earnings smoothing is the technical name for shifting income between periods to make a jagged series look steady, and the verb keeps its plain form with "earnings" as its object. It belongs to the same family as window dressing and creative accounting, all of which describe presentation rather than outright fabrication, and auditors are the natural subject of the doubt.

The phrase names a recognised practice in the terms the profession uses for it, so the sentence holds.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Five lines from a trade-policy digest on barriers, balances and duties. Decide whether each combination is the one trade writing supplies.
statements: Exporters complained that the new certification rules erect non-tariff barriers against processed food.
The ministry announced that it would lay an embargo on timber from the disputed region.
The economy ran a persistent current-account deficit financed by short-term portfolio inflows.
Negotiators agreed to phase out tariffs on industrial goods over a period of seven years.
The commission voted to levy anti-dumping duties on subsidised steel imports.
tasks.solution_overview: Trade writing treats barriers as structures, balances as things a country runs, and duties as charges a state puts on goods, and each of those images fixes its own verb. Check whether the verb belongs to the vocabulary of building, of accounting or of taxation, and whether the state is the party doing it. Only one line borrows a verb from a different family altogether, so compare each phrase with the version a trade ministry would publish.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Exporters complained that the new certification rules erect non-tariff barriers against processed food.**

Barriers are erected, raised or put up, since the metaphor treats them as structures blocking a route to market; the mirror phrase is dismantling or lowering them. Non-tariff barriers are precisely the sort built out of paperwork rather than tax — standards, licences, certification schemes — so a rule about certificates is the natural subject.

The metaphor and the technical term fit together as trade writing normally joins them, so this line stands.

**B) The ministry announced that it would lay an embargo on timber from the disputed region.**

An embargo is imposed on goods, or placed on them, and the same verbs serve sanctions, tariffs and quotas: the state applies a restriction from above. "Lay" belongs to a narrow set of legal and formal objects — lay charges, lay claim to something, lay down conditions — and it has never governed trade restrictions.

**Tip:** Sanctions, embargoes and quotas are all imposed on their target.

The ministry is announcing a ban on a category of imports, so the wording a trade report would carry is "impose an embargo on timber from the disputed region."

**C) The economy ran a persistent current-account deficit financed by short-term portfolio inflows.**

Countries run deficits and surpluses, exactly as companies run losses; the verb turns the balance into something maintained over time rather than a single event. "Persistent" is the standard adjective for a gap that fails to correct itself, and financing by portfolio inflows is the classic description of a deficit covered by volatile capital.

Every element of the phrase belongs to balance-of-payments writing, so the sentence is idiomatic as it stands.

**D) Negotiators agreed to phase out tariffs on industrial goods over a period of seven years.**

Tariffs are phased out when they fall to zero in scheduled steps, and the phrase carries its gradualism inside it, which is why a timetable follows so comfortably. Its partners are the same shape: phase in a rule, phase down a subsidy, with the particle marking the direction of the change.

A schedule stretching over seven years is exactly what this phrasal verb was made to describe, so the line is sound.

**E) The commission voted to levy anti-dumping duties on subsidised steel imports.**

Duties, tariffs and taxes are levied on goods by an authority, and "levy" is the formal member of a set that also includes impose and charge. Anti-dumping duties are the technical response to goods sold below a fair price, so the object of the verb is the standard one and the preposition "on" points at the imports being taxed.

The authority, the charge and the target line up as trade law arranges them, so this wording holds.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Five lines from an audit file and the notes to a set of accounts. Decide whether each phrase is the fixed expression accounting uses.
statements: The auditors issued a qualified opinion after failing to obtain evidence on year-end inventory.
The distributor's collapse forced the group to write off bad debts worth twelve million.
Depreciation on the new fleet is charged on a straight-line basis over eight years.
The group recognises revenue only when control of the goods passes to the customer.
Analysts prefer cash flow because generous accruals can flatter reported earnings.
tasks.solution_overview: Accounting language is close to a legal vocabulary: each procedure has one accepted wording and variation is treated as error. Test each line against what an auditor's report or a note to the accounts would actually say about opinions, irrecoverable balances, depreciation methods and the moment income enters the books. Where a phrase already exists as a term of art, the question is whether the sentence has used it in its proper technical sense.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The auditors issued a qualified opinion after failing to obtain evidence on year-end inventory.**

An audit opinion is issued, and the adjective in front of it is a graded technical scale: unqualified, qualified, adverse, or a disclaimer of opinion. A qualification is exactly what an auditor gives when one area of the accounts cannot be verified, and unverifiable stock is the textbook example, since inventory has to be counted at a moment that has already passed.

**Tip:** Qualified here means limited, not accredited.

The verb, the technical term and the reason given all match audit practice, so this line reads exactly as the report would.

**B) The distributor's collapse forced the group to write off bad debts worth twelve million.**

Debts that will never be collected are written off, which removes them from the books entirely, as against writing an asset down to a lower value that it still carries. "Bad debts" is the settled label for irrecoverable receivables, and a customer's insolvency is the standard trigger for accepting that the money is gone.

A collapse leaves nothing to recover, so the total write-off the sentence describes is the correct treatment and the correct phrase for it.

**C) Depreciation on the new fleet is charged on a straight-line basis over eight years.**

Depreciation is charged, and the method is introduced with "on a straight-line basis" or "on a reducing-balance basis"; the preposition and the article are both fixed inside that formula. Spreading the cost of vehicles evenly across their useful life is the ordinary choice, and eight years is a plausible life for a fleet.

The standard verb, the standard frame for the method and a sensible life all sit together here, so the note is properly worded.

**D) The group recognises revenue only when control of the goods passes to the customer.**

Revenue is recognised, and recognition is the formal act of admitting an item into the financial statements at a particular moment. Modern standards tie that moment to the transfer of control rather than to delivery or invoicing, so "control passes to the customer" is the very test the rule sets out.

The accounting term and the trigger written into the standard appear here in their normal form, so the policy note holds.

**E) Analysts prefer cash flow because generous accruals can flatter reported earnings.**

Figures are flattered when accounting choices make performance look better than the underlying business warrants, and "flatter the numbers" or "flatter earnings" is the usual way of saying it without alleging fraud. Accruals are the standard suspect because they bring income forward and push costs back, which is precisely why analysts fall back on cash.

The verb carries the mild scepticism the sentence needs, and its object is the one it normally takes, so the line is well formed.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Five lines from a corporate-finance memo on a leveraged buyout. Decide whether each phrase is the combination deal reporting actually uses.
statements: The sponsors plan to gear the acquisition with a mixture of senior and mezzanine debt.
Underwriters struggled to float the high-yield notes with institutional buyers.
Covenant packages were designed to ring-fence cash into debt service before dividends.
Rating agencies threatened to place the issuer on credit watch with negative implications.
Management promised to deleverage the balance sheet within eighteen months of closing.
highlights: place the issuer on credit watch
tasks.solution_overview: Leveraged deals speak a dialect of their own: how debt is loaded onto a company, how paper finds buyers, how cash is protected for creditors, and how rating agencies signal concern each have a preferred wording. Ask which verbs take the company or the balance sheet as their object, and which take the securities or the rating itself. Two of the traps borrow a verb from a neighbouring capital-markets ritual, so check whether the object still matches the ceremony you named.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The sponsors plan to gear the acquisition with a mixture of senior and mezzanine debt.**

Companies and balance sheets are geared or leveraged, and a purchase is financed or funded with a given mix of debt; "gear" does not take the acquisition itself as its object. The related noun "gearing" names the resulting ratio, which is why writers talk of high gearing and of a highly geared company rather than of gearing a deal.

**Trap:** Gear the company, finance the acquisition — keep the verb and the object matched.

What the sponsors are loading with borrowed money is the target, so the line a term sheet would carry is "finance the acquisition with a mixture of senior and mezzanine debt."

**B) Underwriters struggled to float the high-yield notes with institutional buyers.**

A company floats when it lists its equity on an exchange, and the noun "flotation" belongs to that IPO ceremony rather than to a bond syndication. High-yield notes are placed with investors, or the issue is syndicated, and both of those verbs describe finding buyers for already designed paper rather than bringing a new company to market.

**Tip:** Float shares in an IPO; place notes in a bond issue.

The underwriters were trying to sell debt to institutions, so the natural wording is "struggled to place the high-yield notes with institutional buyers."

**C) Covenant packages were designed to ring-fence cash into debt service before dividends.**

Cash and assets are ring-fenced from other claims, or earmarked for a particular use; the first pattern protects something against diversion and the second assigns it to a purpose. "Into" belongs to verbs of transfer such as inject and channel, and it cannot follow ring-fence, which is about drawing a protective boundary rather than pouring money somewhere.

The covenants are meant to keep cash reserved for creditors, so the phrase English supplies is either "ring-fence cash from dividend leakage" or "earmark cash for debt service."

**D) Rating agencies threatened to place the issuer on credit watch with negative implications.**

An issuer is placed on credit watch, or put on review for a possible downgrade, and the formula "with negative implications" is the agencies' own stock phrase for the direction of the signal. The wording stops short of an actual cut in the rating, which is exactly the intermediate warning the sentence describes.

The technical ceremony and its fixed wording both appear here in their normal form, so the sentence reads as a ratings bulletin would.

**E) Management promised to deleverage the balance sheet within eighteen months of closing.**

Balance sheets are deleveraged when debt is paid down relative to assets or earnings, and the verb is now standard in post-deal reporting. A timetable after closing is the usual promise sponsors make to rating agencies and lenders, since the leverage that funded the buyout is meant to be temporary.

The verb, the object and the horizon all belong to one familiar frame, so this line holds as written.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Five lines from a competition-authority case file. Decide whether each phrase matches the wording of antitrust and merger review.
statements: Regulators warned that the merger would raise a dominant position in regional logistics.
The authority threatened to open a formal probe into alleged predatory pricing.
Rivals claimed the incumbent had broken a dominant position to shut out new entrants.
Clearance was granted only after the buyer agreed to divest overlapping depots.
The fine was designed to strip the cartelists of their illicit gains.
tasks.solution_overview: Competition writing has a near-legal vocabulary for market power, investigations and remedies, and most of its verbs are fixed. Ask what English says when a firm already holds power and misuses it, what an authority does when it starts an inquiry, and what a buyer must sell to win clearance. One trap borrows a verb that belongs with prices or barriers rather than with dominance itself, so check whether the object still matches the verb's usual family.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Regulators warned that the merger would raise a dominant position in regional logistics.**

A dominant position is created, acquired or strengthened, and EU merger control even prints the paired formula "create or strengthen a dominant position." "Raise" belongs with barriers, concerns, objections and prices — raise a barrier, raise concerns — and it cannot take a market position as its object.

**Trap:** Raise barriers to entry; create or strengthen a dominant position.

The fear in the file is that the merged firm would hold unlawful market power, so the wording a decision would carry is "create or strengthen a dominant position in regional logistics."

**B) The authority threatened to open a formal probe into alleged predatory pricing.**

Investigations, probes and inquiries are opened, and "open a probe into" is the standard journalistic and official pairing for starting one. Predatory pricing is a classic antitrust allegation, so the object of the inquiry is the one competition writing expects.

The verb, the formality marker and the preposition all sit where they should, so this line reads as a case update would.

**C) Rivals claimed the incumbent had broken a dominant position to shut out new entrants.**

What a powerful firm does wrongly is abuse a dominant position, and "abuse of dominance" is the legal label for that offence. "Break" governs laws, rules and agreements — break the law, break a covenant — and a position is held or abused rather than broken.

**Tip:** Break the rules; abuse the position those rules protect against.

The rivals are alleging exclusionary conduct by a powerful incumbent, so the phrase the complaint needs is "abused a dominant position to shut out new entrants."

**D) Clearance was granted only after the buyer agreed to divest overlapping depots.**

Assets are divested when a merger remedy requires their sale, and "divestiture" is the technical name for that cure. Overlapping sites are the classic candidates, because selling them restores a competitor where the overlap would otherwise have removed one.

The remedy verb and the type of asset it takes are exactly the ones merger control uses, so the sentence stands.

**E) The fine was designed to strip the cartelists of their illicit gains.**

Fines and confiscation orders strip offenders of gains, deprive them of profits, or force them to disgorge what they made; all three verbs treat the illicit money as something to be taken away. Cartels are the textbook subject of that logic, since the whole point of the penalty is to make collusion unprofitable.

The verb and the prepositional pattern "strip X of Y" are the ones this remedial purpose calls for, so the wording holds.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Five lines from a macro briefing on fiscal stance and public debt. Decide whether each phrase is the combination public-finance writing uses.
statements: Ministers promised to rein in public spending once the emergency support expired.
The treasury refused to water down the fiscal rules ahead of the autumn statement.
Debt-service costs began to crowd out capital investment in transport and housing.
A sudden stop in foreign buying could trigger a disorderly sell-off in government bonds.
Opposition MPs accused the chancellor of massaging the books to meet the deficit target.
tasks.solution_overview: Public-finance English mixes technical terms of art with a few settled metaphors for restraint, dilution and market stress. Ask what a government does to spending when it wants control, what happens to private investment when public borrowing soaks up savings, and what a bond market does when confidence snaps. One line blends two genuine idioms of fiscal criticism, so check whether the verb and the noun still belong to the same fixed phrase.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Ministers promised to rein in public spending once the emergency support expired.**

Spending is reined in, curbed or brought under control, and "rein in" is the liveliest of those options without leaving the register of serious reporting. Emergency support that is allowed to expire is exactly the moment at which that restraint is usually promised.

The metaphor of holding back a horse and the object "public spending" are a standard pairing in fiscal commentary, so the sentence is sound.

**B) The treasury refused to water down the fiscal rules ahead of the autumn statement.**

Rules, standards and commitments are watered down when their force is diluted, and fiscal rules are a frequent object of that suspicion. Refusing the dilution is the stance a hawkish treasury claims before a budget, so the verb and the political moment fit.

The phrase is the one budget commentary habitually uses for softening a constraint, so this line holds.

**C) Debt-service costs began to crowd out capital investment in transport and housing.**

Crowding out is the textbook name for public borrowing or debt interest absorbing resources that would otherwise fund private or productive investment. Capital spending on infrastructure is the classic victim of that squeeze when interest bills rise.

The technical term and the type of spending it threatens appear here in their normal configuration, so the wording is exact.

**D) A sudden stop in foreign buying could trigger a disorderly sell-off in government bonds.**

Bond markets suffer orderly or disorderly sell-offs, and "disorderly" is the label officials reach for when prices gap and liquidity vanishes. A sudden stop in capital inflows is the standard shock that sets that process off in emerging and advanced markets alike.

Both halves of the sentence — the capital-flow trigger and the market outcome — belong to one established frame, so the line reads as a risk briefing would.

**E) Opposition MPs accused the chancellor of massaging the books to meet the deficit target.**

Two real phrases have been welded together: "massage the figures," which is how budget criticism describes soft presentation of a forecast, and "cook the books," which is the corporate-fraud charge for falsifying accounts. "Massage the books" belongs to neither pattern, and books in the fraud sense are not what a chancellor publishes before a fiscal event.

**Trap:** Blend detection — if each half of the phrase comes from a different idiom, the whole is usually wrong.

The attack is on optimistic presentation of the public finances, so the line that fits the register is "massaging the figures to meet the deficit target."

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Five lines from equity-research notes on valuation and shareholder returns. Decide whether each phrase is the one markets writing supplies.
statements: The shares still trade on a steep premium to the sector on every forward multiple.
Management pledged to reimburse capital to shareholders through buybacks and a special dividend.
A rights issue was floated to plug the hole left by the failed overseas expansion.
The stock re-rated sharply once the new margin targets looked credible to the market.
Analysts warned that a further profit warning could wipe the floor with the rating.
tasks.solution_overview: Equity writing has fixed ways of talking about relative valuation, cash returned to owners, emergency equity raises and changes in how the market prices a stock. Ask which preposition a premium takes, what a company does with surplus cash, and which verbs belong to listing ceremonies rather than to cash calls. One trap imports a sporting idiom into a ratings discussion, so discard anything that could not appear in a sober research note.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The shares still trade on a steep premium to the sector on every forward multiple.**

Shares trade at a premium to a benchmark, or at a discount to it, and that preposition is fixed; the same pattern covers trade at a multiple of earnings. "On" belongs to different market phrases — trade on an exchange, trade on rumour — and it cannot introduce the size of the premium.

**Tip:** Trade at a price, at a premium, at a discount; trade on an exchange.

The comparison with the sector is a valuation gap, so the wording a note would print is "trade at a steep premium to the sector."

**B) Management pledged to reimburse capital to shareholders through buybacks and a special dividend.**

Surplus cash is returned to shareholders, and "return of capital" is the technical label for distributions that are not ordinary dividends. "Reimburse" means paying someone back for an expense they have already met — reimburse travel costs — so it miscasts shareholders as creditors of out-of-pocket spending rather than as owners receiving surplus cash.

Buybacks and special dividends are classic return-of-capital tools, so the sentence needs "return capital to shareholders through buybacks and a special dividend."

**C) A rights issue was floated to plug the hole left by the failed overseas expansion.**

A company floats when it lists, and a flotation is an IPO; a rights issue is launched, announced or underwritten when existing shareholders are offered new stock. "Float" therefore imports the wrong capital-markets ceremony, even though "plug the hole" is an acceptable informal description of repairing a funding gap.

**Trap:** Float the company; launch the rights issue.

The group is raising emergency equity from existing holders, so the natural line is "a rights issue was launched to plug the hole."

**D) The stock re-rated sharply once the new margin targets looked credible to the market.**

A stock re-rates when investors assign it a higher or lower multiple, and the verb is standard in research notes for a lasting change in valuation rather than a one-day move. Credibility of margin targets is exactly the kind of narrative shift that produces a re-rating.

The technical verb and the catalyst both belong to equity commentary, so this line holds.

**E) Analysts warned that a further profit warning could wipe the floor with the rating.**

"Wipe the floor with" means defeat someone comprehensively in a contest, and its home is sport and argument rather than valuation. A rating is hit, cut, or left looking stretched; research English also says a warning would "weigh on the rating" or "put the rating under pressure."

A profit warning is a valuation event, not a contest, so the sober wording is "could weigh heavily on the rating."

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Five lines from a governance briefing on boards, pay and shareholder votes. Decide whether each phrase matches corporate-governance English.
statements: Proxy advisers urged investors to vote down the remuneration report at the annual meeting.
The chair refused to rubber-stamp a related-party deal without an independent fairness opinion.
Succession planning had been deferred for so long that the board risked a leadership vacuum.
Activist funds built a stake large enough to force a seat at the table in strategy talks.
Directors were reminded of their fiduciary duty to act in the company's best interests.
highlights: force a seat at the table
tasks.solution_overview: Governance writing mixes AGM procedure, board oversight metaphors and a few legal terms of art. Test each line against the wording used for pay votes, related-party scrutiny, succession risk and activist pressure. Where a phrase is already a fixture of governance commentary, the only question is whether the sentence has used it in its ordinary sense.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Proxy advisers urged investors to vote down the remuneration report at the annual meeting.**

A resolution is voted down when shareholders reject it, and the remuneration report is the classic target of that protest in markets with an advisory say-on-pay vote. Proxy advisers are precisely the intermediaries who issue that recommendation ahead of the AGM.

The verb, the report and the meeting all belong to one settled AGM frame, so the sentence is idiomatic as written.

**B) The chair refused to rubber-stamp a related-party deal without an independent fairness opinion.**

Rubber-stamping is the settled metaphor for approving something without real scrutiny, and refusing to do it is how serious boards describe their oversight role. Related-party deals are the textbook case that demand independent review, and a fairness opinion is the document that review often produces.

The sceptical metaphor and the transaction type fit together as governance writing joins them, so this line stands.

**C) Succession planning had been deferred for so long that the board risked a leadership vacuum.**

A leadership vacuum is the standard label for the gap that opens when a chief executive leaves without a ready successor. Linking that risk to deferred succession planning is the warning governance reports issue when boards have failed to groom a replacement.

The metaphor and the cause are the ones this failure routinely attracts, so the wording holds.

**D) Activist funds built a stake large enough to force a seat at the table in strategy talks.**

Activists build stakes, amass positions or accumulate shares, and "a seat at the table" is the usual prize they then demand in board or strategy discussions. "Force" correctly marks that the invitation is extracted rather than offered.

Both the stake-building verb and the access metaphor are fixtures of activist coverage, so the sentence reads as a briefing would.

**E) Directors were reminded of their fiduciary duty to act in the company's best interests.**

Fiduciary duty is the legal term for the obligation of loyalty and care directors owe the company, and "act in the company's best interests" is the plain-English restatement that accompanies it. The reminder is a stock move in governance training and in board minutes when conflicts loom.

The legal label and its gloss appear here in their normal pairing, so the line is exact.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five lines from a banking and credit-risk briefing. Decide whether each phrase is the combination credit writing uses.
statements: Rising defaults forced the bank to take larger provisions against its corporate book.
The syndicate was oversubscribed within hours of the order book opening.
Covenant-lite loans left lenders with little room to pull the plug at the first sign of stress.
Stress tests asked whether capital buffers could withstand a severe downturn.
The regulator ordered the lender to set aside more capital to cover concentration risk.
highlights: set aside more capital to cover
tasks.solution_overview: Credit and banking English distinguishes provisions, syndication demand, covenant strength and capital held against risk, and each idea has a preferred verb. Ask what a bank does when it expects losses, what happens when a loan is popular with lenders, and how capital relates to the risks it is meant to absorb. One colourful phrase is accepted market slang; another only looks technical, so test each line against what a credit memo would actually print.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Rising defaults forced the bank to take larger provisions against its corporate book.**

Banks make, book or raise provisions for expected losses, and "provision against" is the pattern that names the exposure being covered. "Take" does not govern provisions in credit English, even though speakers take a charge or take a hit; the accounting act itself is making or booking the provision.

**Tip:** Make a provision; take a charge.

Defaults are exactly what drive higher expected-loss numbers, so the line should read "make larger provisions against its corporate book."

**B) The syndicate was oversubscribed within hours of the order book opening.**

An issue or an order book is oversubscribed when demand exceeds the amount on offer; the syndicate is the group of banks arranging the deal, not the thing investors subscribe for. Saying the syndicate was oversubscribed confuses the arrangers with the paper they are selling.

**Trap:** Oversubscribe the issue or the book, not the syndicate that runs it.

What filled too fast was demand for the loan, so the natural wording is "the issue was oversubscribed" or "the order book was oversubscribed."

**C) Covenant-lite loans left lenders with little room to pull the plug at the first sign of stress.**

"Pull the plug" is accepted credit slang for cutting a facility or forcing a default once protections are breached, and covenant-lite structures are defined by how little of that power they leave. The colourful verb is therefore doing exact technical work here rather than drifting into journalism.

The contrast between thin covenants and limited enforcement power is the standard critique of these loans, so the sentence stands.

**D) Stress tests asked whether capital buffers could withstand a severe downturn.**

Buffers withstand, absorb or weather a shock, and stress tests are built to ask exactly that question under a severe scenario. "Severe downturn" is the usual label for the adverse case those tests apply.

The verb, the buffer and the scenario form one settled supervisory frame, so this line is sound.

**E) The regulator ordered the lender to set aside more capital to cover concentration risk.**

Banks hold or maintain capital against risks, and supervisors require them to hold additional capital for concentrations; "set aside … to cover" is closer to provisioning language than to the capital stack. Capital is not an expense put on one side for a bill, but a permanent cushion measured against risk-weighted assets.

The order is about the capital requirement, so the phrasing a rulebook would use is "hold more capital against concentration risk."

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five lines from strategy notes on diversification, scale and competitive advantage. Decide whether each phrase matches strategy writing.
statements: The conglomerate vowed to stick to its knitting after two ill-judged foreign acquisitions.
Scale advantages allowed the platform to undercut rivals on price without sacrificing service.
Managers hoped the new brand would cannibalise sales from the group's older products overnight.
A first-mover advantage proved short-lived once imitators flooded the niche.
The board approved a bolt-on acquisition to deepen the firm's presence in diagnostics.
tasks.solution_overview: Strategy commentary leans on a handful of metaphors for focus, pricing power, product overlap and deal size. Ask which phrases praise discipline, which describe deliberate self-competition, and which label a small deal meant to deepen a franchise. One trap is a folk idiom that sounds businesslike but is not the settled strategy phrase, and another treats a harmful side-effect as if it were the aim.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The conglomerate vowed to stick to its knitting after two ill-judged foreign acquisitions.**

The established strategy idiom is "stick to the knitting," not "stick to its knitting": the definite article is part of the fixed phrase, which means concentrate on the core business. Swapping in a possessive looks only slightly off, but it breaks the idiom that management commentary actually prints.

**Trap:** Stick to the knitting is fossilised with the.

After failed diversification the promise is a return to the core, so the line needs "stick to the knitting."

**B) Scale advantages allowed the platform to undercut rivals on price without sacrificing service.**

Rivals are undercut on price when a firm can charge less, and scale is the classic source of that ability. The pairing is so standard that "undercut on price" barely needs glossing in a strategy note.

Cost advantage and the pricing verb match exactly here, so the wording holds.

**C) Managers hoped the new brand would cannibalise sales from the group's older products overnight.**

Cannibalisation is usually a risk to be managed, not a hope to be celebrated: firms worry that a new product will cannibalise existing sales. Treating overnight cannibalisation as the desired outcome reverses the evaluation the verb carries in strategy English.

**Tip:** Cannibalise names damage to your own franchise, not a target to aim at.

If the goal is migration, writers speak of switching customers or replacing the old line; they do not hope to cannibalise it overnight, so this line fails.

**D) A first-mover advantage proved short-lived once imitators flooded the niche.**

First-mover advantage is the textbook label for the head start an early entrant enjoys, and saying it proved short-lived is the standard follow-up when copycats arrive. Flooding a niche is the usual image for that rush of imitators.

The technical term and the way it erodes appear here in their normal pairing, so the sentence is sound.

**E) The board approved a bolt-on acquisition to deepen the firm's presence in diagnostics.**

A bolt-on acquisition is a small, complementary deal added to an existing platform, as opposed to a transformative merger. Deepening presence in a known segment is precisely the purpose that label describes.

Deal-size jargon and strategic intent line up as M&A commentary expects, so this line stands.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Five lines from a supply-chain and trade-finance digest. Decide whether each phrase is the fixed combination logistics and trade credit use.
statements: Port congestion began to seal off shipments of intermediate goods into the assembly hubs.
Importers arranged a letter of credit to secure payment against shipping documents.
The manufacturer dual-sourced critical chips to hedge against a single-supplier failure.
Retailers' lean inventories left no buffer when the upstream shock hit.
Freight rates spiked as carriers blanked sailings to ration scarce vessel space.
tasks.solution_overview: Supply-chain English mixes physical metaphors for blockage with the technical vocabulary of trade finance, sourcing and shipping schedules. Ask what congestion does to flows, how payment is secured against documents, and what carriers do to vessel capacity when rates are rising. One trap borrows a security verb that seals areas rather than choking cargo flows, so check whether the metaphor still matches a logistics scene.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Port congestion began to seal off shipments of intermediate goods into the assembly hubs.**

Areas, streets and crime scenes are sealed off; cargo flows are choked, disrupted or held up. "Seal off" pictures a cordon that people cannot cross, which is the wrong physical image for containers waiting outside a clogged harbour.

**Trap:** Seal off a zone; choke or disrupt a flow of goods.

Congestion is strangling movement rather than cordoning a place, so logistics writing would say "choke the flow of shipments into the assembly hubs."

**B) Importers arranged a letter of credit to secure payment against shipping documents.**

A letter of credit is the standard trade-finance instrument that promises payment when stipulated documents are presented, and "against shipping documents" is the classic formulation of that condition. Importers are the party that typically arranges it in favour of the exporter.

The instrument, the purpose and the documentary trigger are exactly as trade finance words them, so this line holds.

**C) The manufacturer dual-sourced critical chips to hedge against a single-supplier failure.**

Dual-sourcing is the settled term for splitting orders across two suppliers, and hedging against single-supplier failure is the textbook reason for doing it. Critical components such as chips are the usual example in resilience notes.

The sourcing verb and the risk it addresses match as strategy for supply risk expects, so the sentence is sound.

**D) Retailers' lean inventories left no buffer when the upstream shock hit.**

Inventories are lean when stock is kept deliberately thin, and the whole point of that model is the missing buffer the sentence names. An upstream shock is the standard event that then exposes the fragility.

The lean-inventory label and its consequence appear here in their ordinary coupling, so the wording holds.

**E) Freight rates spiked as carriers blanked sailings to ration scarce vessel space.**

Carriers blank sailings when they cancel scheduled voyages to tighten capacity, and the verb is now standard in shipping reports. Rationing scarce vessel space is precisely the effect those blankings produce when demand still exceeds supply.

The technical shipping verb and the capacity logic belong together, so this line is exact.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Five lines from a restructuring and insolvency memo. Decide whether each phrase matches distress and turnaround English.
statements: Creditors agreed to a debt-for-equity swap that left the founders with a minority stake.
The company filed for creditor protection after talks on a standstill agreement collapsed.
Advisers warned that fire-sale disposals would crystallise losses across the portfolio.
A white knight emerged with a rescue bid pitched above the liquidation value.
Lenders threatened to accelerate the debt if the interest cover covenant was breached.
tasks.solution_overview: Distress vocabulary is highly conventional: exchanges of paper for ownership, pauses in enforcement, forced sales, rescue bidders and the right to call loans early each have a name. Test whether each line has used the term of art in the situation that term was coined for. Where the label already encodes the legal or market move, little else in the sentence needs to carry the meaning.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Creditors agreed to a debt-for-equity swap that left the founders with a minority stake.**

A debt-for-equity swap converts claims into shares, and leaving founders diluted to a minority is the usual political price of that rescue. The hyphenated label is the fixed name for the exchange rather than a loose description.

The instrument and the ownership outcome match as restructuring memos describe them, so the sentence stands.

**B) The company filed for creditor protection after talks on a standstill agreement collapsed.**

A standstill agreement freezes enforcement while a deal is negotiated, and filing for creditor protection is the court route taken when those talks fail. Both phrases are terms of art in insolvency practice, and the sequence — failed standstill, then filing — is the standard narrative.

The two technical moves appear in the order distress stories expect, so this line holds.

**C) Advisers warned that fire-sale disposals would crystallise losses across the portfolio.**

Losses are crystallised when a sale turns a paper decline into a realised one, and a fire sale is the forced disposal that does exactly that. Portfolio-wide crystallisation is the warning turnaround teams issue when hurried exits are proposed.

The accounting verb and the forced-sale noun belong to one familiar pair, so the wording is exact.

**D) A white knight emerged with a rescue bid pitched above the liquidation value.**

A white knight is the friendly rescuer in a contested or distressed situation, and pitching a bid above liquidation value is how such a bid is justified to creditors. The chess metaphor is fully lexicalised in M&A and restructuring English.

The label, the purpose and the valuation floor line up as deal reporting joins them, so the sentence is sound.

**E) Lenders threatened to accelerate the debt if the interest cover covenant was breached.**

Acceleration makes the whole loan immediately due after a default, and an interest-cover breach is a classic trigger. "Accelerate the debt" is the lenders' own wording for that contractual right.

The remedy and the covenant that unlocks it are exactly as a facility agreement arranges them, so this line holds.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five lines from FX and capital-flow commentary. Decide whether each phrase is the combination markets and macro writing use.
statements: Heavy intervention failed to put a floor under the currency once reserves looked thin.
Portfolio managers rotated into defensive sectors as risk appetite dried away.
A carry trade dismantled abruptly when the funding currency began to appreciate.
Officials denied they were speaking down the exchange rate to help exporters.
Hot money flooded towards the local bond market in search of yield.
tasks.solution_overview: FX commentary depends on a few metaphors for supporting a rate, for risk appetite, for leveraged currency bets and for volatile foreign inflows. Ask which verbs keep a currency from falling further, what appetite does when it disappears, and which phrases belong to official rhetoric about the exchange rate. Several traps are near-miss particles or support verbs, so listen for the exact companion word the metaphor requires.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Heavy intervention failed to put a floor under the currency once reserves looked thin.**

Central banks try to put a floor under a currency, or under asset prices, when they buy to stop a freefall; the metaphor treats the rate as something that needs a base. Thin reserves are exactly why that defence then fails.

The support metaphor and the constraint on it are the ones FX desks use, so this line is sound.

**B) Portfolio managers rotated into defensive sectors as risk appetite dried away.**

Risk appetite dries up, not away; "dry up" is the fixed phrasal verb for a source that fails, while "dry away" is not an English pattern at all. Rotation into defensive sectors is the right accompanying move, so only the particle is wrong.

**Trap:** Dry up for vanishing supply or appetite; there is no dry away.

The sentence needs "as risk appetite dried up."

**C) A carry trade dismantled abruptly when the funding currency began to appreciate.**

Carry trades unwind when positions are closed in a hurry, and unwind is the market's own verb for that reversal. "Dismantle" governs machines, barriers and organisations — dismantle a scaffold, dismantle a cartel — and it never takes a trade as its object.

Appreciation of the funding currency is the classic trigger, so the line should read "a carry trade unwound abruptly when the funding currency began to appreciate."

**D) Officials denied they were speaking down the exchange rate to help exporters.**

The fixed phrase is talk down the currency, or talk the currency down: officials use words rather than intervention to push a rate lower. "Speak down" is not a capital-markets pattern, even though speak and talk overlap in everyday English.

**Tip:** Talk down a currency; talk up a stock — the verb is talk, not speak.

The denial concerns jawboning for a weaker rate, so the wording markets expect is "talking down the exchange rate."

**E) Hot money flooded towards the local bond market in search of yield.**

Hot money floods into a market, pours into it or flows into it; the preposition marks entry across the border into the asset class. "Towards" only signals direction without arrival, which is too weak for the surge the sentence wants to describe.

Yield-seeking foreign inflows are the classic hot-money story, so the phrase needs "flooded into the local bond market."

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Five lines from labour-economics notes on bargaining, hours and participation. Decide whether each phrase is the one specialist labour writing supplies.
statements: Unions threatened to ballot members on industrial action after talks stalled.
A higher reservation wage kept some claimants out of low-paid vacancies.
Employers tried to buy out restrictive practices with a one-off productivity bonus.
The participation rate edged higher as childcare places expanded in cities.
Zero-hours contracts left many workers unable to smooth their weekly earnings.
tasks.solution_overview: Labour economics has a precise vocabulary for strike procedure, the lowest acceptable wage, outdated work rules and measured labour-force entry. Ask which verbs belong with a strike ballot, what a reservation wage actually is, and how participation is reported when it moves only a little. One trap looks like industrial-relations English but uses the wrong support verb for ending a practice.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Unions threatened to ballot members on industrial action after talks stalled.**

Unions ballot members for industrial action, or hold a ballot on strike action; the preposition that introduces the action is for, not on, when ballot is the verb. "Ballot on" appears with the noun — a ballot on strike action — but the verb pattern is ballot someone for something.

**Trap:** A ballot on X; ballot members for X.

After stalled talks the threat is a strike vote, so the line should read "ballot members for industrial action."

**B) A higher reservation wage kept some claimants out of low-paid vacancies.**

The reservation wage is the technical name for the lowest pay a worker will accept, and a higher one is exactly what keeps people out of poorly paid jobs. Claimants and vacancies are the usual cast in that explanation.

The term of art and the mechanism it names appear here correctly, so the sentence holds.

**C) Employers tried to buy out restrictive practices with a one-off productivity bonus.**

Restrictive practices are bought off, or management buys the abandonment of them; "buy out" governs owners and partners — buy out a shareholder, a buyout — rather than work rules. The productivity bonus is the right sort of sweetener, so only the verb is wrong.

**Tip:** Buy out equity; buy off resistance to change.

The deal is payment for giving up old rules, so industrial-relations English prefers "buy off restrictive practices."

**D) The participation rate edged higher as childcare places expanded in cities.**

Participation rates rise, fall or edge higher, and "edge" correctly marks a small move. Expanded childcare is a classic supply-side reason given for higher female participation in particular.

The statistical verb of small change and the policy cause fit labour-force commentary, so this line is sound.

**E) Zero-hours contracts left many workers unable to smooth their weekly earnings.**

Households and workers smooth earnings or consumption when they keep spending steady despite lumpy income; the verb is standard in labour and macroeconomics. Zero-hours contracts are precisely the arrangement that makes that smoothing hard because hours jump from week to week.

The technical verb and the contract type that frustrates it belong together, so the wording holds.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Five lines from a regulatory-compliance and conduct briefing. Decide whether each phrase matches supervision and enforcement English.
statements: The watchdog threatened to throw the book at firms that mis-sold complex products.
Compliance teams scrambled to close out gaps ahead of the new disclosure rule.
A deferred prosecution agreement let the bank escape a full criminal trial.
Supervisors required the firm to remediate weaknesses in its financial-crime controls.
Whistleblowers are protected when they escalate concerns through approved channels.
tasks.solution_overview: Conduct and compliance writing mixes enforcement colour with precise verbs for fixing controls and raising alarms. Ask which phrases a regulator's press notice would actually print, what firms do to gaps before a rule bites, and how weaknesses in controls are formally repaired. Two traps sound forceful but belong to tabloid crime reporting or to trading desks rather than to supervisory English.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The watchdog threatened to throw the book at firms that mis-sold complex products.**

"Throw the book at" is tabloid and police-drama English for maximum punishment; regulators impose fines, take enforcement action or pursue the full range of sanctions. Mis-selling is a real conduct offence, but the colourful idiom is not how supervision writes its threats.

**Trap:** Register failure — if it could headline a crime show, it probably does not belong in a regulatory brief.

The watchdog is promising tough enforcement, so the sober line is "take the full range of enforcement action against firms that mis-sold complex products."

**B) Compliance teams scrambled to close out gaps ahead of the new disclosure rule.**

Gaps in controls are closed or remediated; "close out" is trading and derivatives English for terminating a position — close out a trade, close out a hedge. Importing that particle into compliance work produces a blend that neither desk would print.

**Tip:** Close out a position; close a control gap.

Teams preparing for a new rule need to "close gaps" or "remediate gaps" in their disclosures.

**C) A deferred prosecution agreement let the bank escape a full criminal trial.**

Deferred prosecution agreements are real tools, but they resolve or settle potential charges; they do not "let" a bank "escape" in the wording counsel would use, and more importantly the collocation under test is strained because DPAs are entered into or reached, not pictured as jailbreaks. The sensational verb escape belongs to crime reporting rather than to the settlement vocabulary of "enter into a DPA" or "resolve charges through a DPA."

The instrument is named correctly, yet the support verb around it is journalistic rather than legal, so the line fails as specialist collocation — prefer "the bank entered into a deferred prosecution agreement rather than face a full criminal trial."

**D) Supervisors required the firm to remediate weaknesses in its financial-crime controls.**

Weaknesses are remediated in supervisory English, and financial-crime controls are a standard object of that order. The verb is more formal than fix or repair and is the one examination letters actually use.

The supervisory verb and the control area match as a consent order would word them, so this line holds.

**E) Whistleblowers are protected when they escalate concerns through approved channels.**

Concerns are escalated through a chain of command or through approved channels, and whistleblower policies are built around that escalation path. Protection attached to proper escalation is the usual legal and corporate framing.

The verb, the object and the channel phrase are the ones compliance manuals print, so the sentence is sound.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Five lines from project-finance and infrastructure notes. Decide whether each phrase is the combination that sector uses.
statements: Lenders refused to take out construction risk until the plant had passed acceptance tests.
The concession agreement locked in tariffs for the first fifteen years of operation.
Sponsors injected additional equity to cure a cash-flow shortfall during ramp-up.
A take-or-pay clause obliged the offtaker to pay even when volumes fell short.
Political-risk insurance was bought to cover expropriation and contract frustration.
tasks.solution_overview: Project finance has a ritual vocabulary for who bears construction risk, how tariffs are fixed, how equity plugs holes and how offtake is guaranteed. Ask which verbs mean assuming a risk, which mean fixing a price, and which name the contract forms that keep lenders whole. One trap uses an insurance verb for a risk-allocation idea that term sheets express differently.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Lenders refused to take out construction risk until the plant had passed acceptance tests.**

Parties take on risk, assume it or are left with it; "take out" belongs to insurance — take out a policy — and to removing something. Construction risk passes from sponsors to contractors or remains with sponsors until completion tests, but nobody takes it out.

**Trap:** Take out insurance; take on risk.

Lenders are refusing to bear unfinished-plant risk, so the term-sheet wording is "refused to take on construction risk until the plant had passed acceptance tests."

**B) The concession agreement locked in tariffs for the first fifteen years of operation.**

Tariffs, prices and rates are locked in when a contract fixes them against later change, and concession agreements are the usual place that fix appears for infrastructure. A fifteen-year window is a typical availability period for that protection.

The verb and the regulated price it freezes are standard project-finance English, so this line holds.

**C) Sponsors injected additional equity to cure a cash-flow shortfall during ramp-up.**

Equity is injected when sponsors put fresh capital in, and shortfalls are cured in facility-agreement English when a breach or gap is repaired. Ramp-up is the phase when volumes are still climbing and cash is often tight.

Both technical verbs sit in their normal slots here, so the sentence is sound.

**D) A take-or-pay clause obliged the offtaker to pay even when volumes fell short.**

Take-or-pay is the fixed name for an offtake obligation to pay for capacity whether or not it is used, and it exists precisely for the shortfall case the sentence describes. The offtaker is the party bound by that clause.

The contract label and its economic effect match exactly, so this wording stands.

**E) Political-risk insurance was bought to cover expropriation and contract frustration.**

Political-risk insurance is the product that covers expropriation, currency inconvertibility and related sovereign events, and buying cover for those perils is how sponsors describe the purchase. Contract frustration sits inside the same family of covered political events.

The product name and the perils listed are the ones underwriters catalogue, so the line is exact.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Five lines from a monetary-transmission and yield-curve briefing. Decide whether each phrase matches advanced macro-finance English.
statements: A steeper yield curve usually signals that markets are pricing in firmer growth ahead.
Quantitative tightening began to drain excess reserves from the banking system.
Forward guidance was recalibrated to avoid a premature easing of financial conditions.
Mortgage spreads widened as lenders passed on higher wholesale funding costs.
The policy rate was held in restrictive territory to keep demand in check.
highlights: passed on higher wholesale funding costs
tasks.solution_overview: Advanced macro-finance writing treats the curve, the balance sheet, guidance and credit spreads as parts of one transmission story. Ask how markets embed a growth view in prices, what tightening does to reserves, and where a policy rate sits when it is meant to cool demand. Each line here turns on a phrase that is already a term of art in central-bank and rates commentary.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A steeper yield curve usually signals that markets are pricing in firmer growth ahead.**

Markets price in an outcome when its probability is already reflected in asset prices, and firmer growth is a classic thing a steepening curve is said to price in. The phrasal verb is indispensable in rates commentary.

The curve signal and the pricing-in verb belong to one standard reading of steepening, so this line holds.

**B) Quantitative tightening began to drain excess reserves from the banking system.**

Tightening drains reserves when the central bank shrinks its balance sheet, and excess reserves are the precise stock being reduced. The plumbing verb drain is the one operations notes use for that shrinkage.

The policy label and the reserve effect match as balance-sheet policy describes them, so the sentence is sound.

**C) Forward guidance was recalibrated to avoid a premature easing of financial conditions.**

Financial conditions ease or tighten, and guidance is recalibrated when the committee resets what it wants markets to infer. Avoiding premature easing is a standard hawkish reason for adjusting that language.

Both halves — the guidance verb and the conditions noun phrase — are fixtures of policy writing, so the wording stands.

**D) Mortgage spreads widened as lenders passed on higher wholesale funding costs.**

Costs are passed on to customers when lenders raise retail rates in step with wholesale ones, and spreads widen when that pass-through is incomplete or lagged. The two movements are the usual pairing in credit-channel notes.

The pass-on verb and the spread outcome are exactly how transmission into mortgages is narrated, so this line is exact.

**E) The policy rate was held in restrictive territory to keep demand in check.**

A rate sits in restrictive territory when it is judged above neutral and is cooling the economy, and keeping demand in check is the purpose of staying there. Both phrases are now stock central-bank English.

The locative metaphor for stance and the demand objective fit together as a policy explanation would, so the sentence holds.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Five lines from advanced trade and industrial-policy analysis. Decide whether each phrase is the specialist combination the field uses.
statements: Critics argued that local-content rules would fragment global value chains beyond repair.
Export credits were deployed to level the playing field against subsidised rivals.
The ministry announced a strategic stockpile to ride out disruptions in critical minerals.
Dumping margins were calculated by comparing export prices against normal value.
Supporters claimed the tariff would raise infant industries until they reached scale.
highlights: fragment global value chains beyond repair
tasks.solution_overview: Industrial-policy English mixes value-chain analysis, subsidy counter-measures, stockpiles and anti-dumping arithmetic. Ask which metaphors describe breaking up production networks, what export credits are said to do to competition, and which verbs belong with infant-industry protection. Several lines are almost right but tip into overstatement or the wrong preposition, so judge the whole phrase rather than the familiar noun alone.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Critics argued that local-content rules would fragment global value chains beyond repair.**

Value chains fragment, or production fragments across borders, and that verb is sound; the failure is the tacked-on "beyond repair," which belongs to relationships and damaged objects rather than to supply networks that can be reconfigured. Specialist critique stops at fragment, reshape or shorten global value chains.

**Trap:** Beyond repair intensifies emotion but is not part of the trade collocation.

The charge against local-content rules is fragmentation, so the line should end at "fragment global value chains" without the irreversible flourish.

**B) Export credits were deployed to level the playing field against subsidised rivals.**

A playing field is levelled, but the complement is between rivals or for domestic firms — not against them. "Against" turns the metaphor into a weapon pointed at competitors, whereas the idiom means restoring fairness among them.

**Tip:** Level the playing field for X / between X and Y — never against.

Export credits as a counter-subsidy need "level the playing field with subsidised rivals" or "for domestic exporters facing subsidised rivals."

**C) The ministry announced a strategic stockpile to ride out disruptions in critical minerals.**

Countries ride out disruptions, shocks and storms when buffers let them endure a temporary shortage, and a strategic stockpile is built for exactly that purpose in critical minerals. The phrasal verb is standard resilience English.

The stockpile and the disruptions it is meant to survive belong together, so this wording holds.

**D) Dumping margins were calculated by comparing export prices against normal value.**

Anti-dumping calculations compare the export price with normal value, or set the margin as the difference between those two; "compare against" is not the statutory or textbook preposition. "Against" belongs to benchmarks in other settings — performance against a target — and it jars in the dumping formula.

The arithmetic is right in spirit, so the repaired line is "comparing export prices with normal value."

**E) Supporters claimed the tariff would raise infant industries until they reached scale.**

Infant industries are protected, fostered or sheltered under the infant-industry argument; "raise" governs children, funds and objections — raise a child, raise capital, raise an objection — and it does not take an industry as the thing cultivated behind a tariff wall.

**Trap:** Raise capital for an industry; protect an infant industry.

The classic case for temporary tariffs needs "protect infant industries until they reached scale."

tasks.title: Task 21
tasks.context: Five lines from advanced corporate-governance and capital-structure analysis. Decide whether each phrase is the specialist combination boards and bondholders use.
statements: Independent directors were asked to form a special committee to opine on the related-party offer.
Bondholders complained that asset stripping had hollowed out their recovery prospects.
The dual-class structure entrenched founders against a hostile change of control.
Covenant carve-outs let the issuer leak value to equity through permitted distributions.
A poison pill was adopted to dilute any bidder who crossed the trigger threshold.
tasks.solution_overview: Governance and leveraged-structure English has fixed ways of describing special committees, tunnelling of value, dual-class control and takeover defences. Ask which verbs boards use for formal opinions, what asset stripping does to creditors, and how poison pills actually work. Two traps are near-miss prepositions or support verbs around otherwise genuine terms of art.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Independent directors were asked to form a special committee to opine on the related-party offer.**

Special committees opine on conflicted transactions, and "opine on" is the slightly formal verb minutes and fairness opinions still use. Related-party offers are the classic trigger for that committee structure.

The committee, the verb and the conflicted deal type match Delaware-style governance English, so this line holds.

**B) Bondholders complained that asset stripping had hollowed out their recovery prospects.**

Asset stripping is a real charge, but the fixed creditor complaint is that it has hollowed out the company or the collateral, not the abstract "recovery prospects." Prospects are damaged, impaired or weakened; hollow out takes a structure that once had substance — a firm, a balance sheet, a franchise.

**Trap:** Hollow out the company; impair recovery prospects.

Bondholders fear empty collateral, so the natural line is "asset stripping had hollowed out the company" or "had impaired their recovery prospects."

**C) The dual-class structure entrenched founders against a hostile change of control.**

Dual-class shares entrench founders, and entrenchment is the standard critique, but the preposition is wrong: founders are entrenched in control, or the structure entrenches them; "against" belongs to protect against or insure against. The hostile change of control is what the structure resists, yet English does not entrench someone against an event.

The repaired governance line is "entrenched founders in the face of a hostile change of control" or simply "entrenched founder control."

**D) Covenant carve-outs let the issuer leak value to equity through permitted distributions.**

Value leaks to equity when loopholes allow cash or assets to leave the restricted group, and covenant carve-outs are exactly those loopholes. Distressed-debt analysts use "leak value" as a term of art for that transfer.

The carve-out mechanism and the leakage metaphor belong together in bondholder English, so the sentence stands.

**E) A poison pill was adopted to dilute any bidder who crossed the trigger threshold.**

A poison pill is adopted or implemented, and its mechanical effect is to dilute a bidder who crosses a ownership trigger. Both the adoption verb and the dilution purpose are the textbook description of a shareholder-rights plan.

The defence and its trigger logic appear here as takeover manuals state them, so this wording holds.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Five lines from derivatives and risk-management notes. Decide whether each phrase matches specialist market-risk English.
statements: The desk rolled the hedge forward into the next quarter to keep duration matched.
Counterparties posted variation margin as mark-to-market losses mounted.
Managers tried to diversify away idiosyncratic risk by holding a single concentrated name.
A wrong-way risk arose because the guarantor's credit improved as the underlying deteriorated.
The fund was caught on a short squeeze as borrowed stock became scarce and expensive.
tasks.solution_overview: Derivatives English is exact about rolling hedges, posting margin, diversifying risk and the directionality of credit exposures. Ask what a desk does when a hedge expires, what counterparties deliver as prices move, and whether a described portfolio could possibly diversify anything. Two traps state a genuine term of art in a situation that contradicts its definition, and one uses the wrong particle with a squeeze.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The desk rolled the hedge forward into the next quarter to keep duration matched.**

Hedges are rolled forward when an expiring contract is replaced with a later one, and keeping duration matched is the usual reason. The particle "forward" is part of the fixed dealing phrase.

The roll and the duration motive are exactly how rates desks narrate that maintenance, so this line holds.

**B) Counterparties posted variation margin as mark-to-market losses mounted.**

Variation margin is posted as mark-to-market moves against a party, and mounting losses are the trigger. "Post margin" is the operational verb clearing houses and CSAs use.

The collateral verb and the MTM cause match market practice, so the sentence is sound.
